item.base_system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr powder blend (Ti, ZrH2, HfH2, Nb, TaH0.5) in ink form
item.intervention: Hydrogenation of extruded ink at 730 °C for 2 h under pure hydrogen to form hydride powders
item.processing: Hydrogenation at 730 °C for 2 h under pure hydrogen
item.test_conditions: In situ X-ray diffraction under vacuum from 100 to 1000 °C
item.structure_change: Formation of hydride phases: TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5
quotes: The hydride powder blend is obtained after hydrogenating of an extruded ink at 730 °C for 2 h, using pure hydrogen.
As shown in Figure 2 a,b , subsequent dehydrogenation of the powder blend under vacuum takes place between 300 and 750 °C.

item.base_system: Hydride powder blend (TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5)
item.intervention: Heating under vacuum to decompose hydrides sequentially
item.processing: In situ X-ray diffraction heating from 100 to 1000 °C under vacuum
item.structure_change: Sequential decomposition: TaH0.5 and NbH decompose at ≈290 °C; TiH2 at ≈545 °C; HfH2 at ≈460 °C; ZrH2 at ≈720 °C; formation of β-BCC and α-HCP phases
item.attributed_mechanism: Decomposition sequence follows hydride formation enthalpy values; Nb and Ta act as β-stabilizers for Ti, decreasing allotropic temperature
quotes: The sequence of the hydrides decomposition closely follows the sequence of hydride formation enthalpy values for Ta (−34 kJ mol−1), Nb (−40 kJ mol−1), Hf (−64 kJ mol−1), Ti (−67 kJ mol−1), and Zr (−79 kJ mol−1).
The absence of α‐Ti indicates that Nb and Ta (which are β‐stabilizer for Ti) are already alloyed with the nascent Ti, thus decreasing the allotropic temperature.

item.base_system: De-bound ink ingot (loosely packed powder blend)
item.intervention: Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 0.25 h (15 min)
item.structure_change: Microstructure remains porous; consists of three metallic phases: (Ti,Nb,Ta)-rich (β-BCC1), (Zr,Hf)-rich (α-HCP), and Ta-rich; presence of (Zr,Hf)O2 and HfC particles
item.attributed_mechanism: Low Ta diffusivity leads to large agglomerates; (Zr,Hf)O2 forms due to oxygen contamination; HfC forms due to carbon contamination
quotes: The undiffused Ta‐rich phases are consistent with the occurrence of large agglomerates of Ta powders and their low ability to homogenize with the other metallic phases, due to the low Ta diffusivity.

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: De-bound ink ingot (loosely packed powder blend). Intervention: Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 0.25 h (15 min). Processing: Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 15 min. Test conditions: Vacuum, 1400 °C. Structure change: Microstructure remains porous; consists of three metallic phases: (Ti,Nb,Ta)-rich (β-BCC1), (Zr,Hf)-rich (α-HCP), and Ta-rich; presence of (Zr,Hf)O2 and HfC particles. Mechanism: Low Ta diffusivity leads to large agglomerates; (Zr,Hf)O2 forms due to oxygen contamination; HfC forms due to carbon contamination. Evidence: measured. Quote: "The undiffused Ta‐rich phases are consistent with the occurrence of large agglomerates of Ta powders and their low ability to homogenize with the other metallic phases, due to the low Ta diffusivity."

item.intervention: Extended vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h
item.structure_change: Nearly fully densified (99.7 ± 0.2% relative density); large linear shrinkage of 23.5 ± 0.1%; formation of second β-BCC phase (BCC2) around α-HCP phase
item.attributed_mechanism: Ta diffused into surrounding metallic phases over longer time; densification occurs with time
quotes: Finally, after sintering for the longest time (18 h), the microstructure is nearly fully densified, consistent with a high relative density of 99.7 ± 0.2% and a large linear shrinkage of 23.5 ± 0.1%.
After sintering for a longer time (4 h), the microstructure is further densified, and the Ta‐rich phases are smaller, as Ta diffused into the surrounding metallic phases for a longer time.
A second β‐BCC phase (BCC2) is visible in the XRD spectra and the SEM‐BSE micrographs in Figure 2e.

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Sintered HfNbTaTiZr (1400 °C, 4 h). Intervention: Extended vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h. Processing: Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h. Quote: "Finally, after sintering for the longest time (18 h), the microstructure is nearly fully densified, consistent with a high relative density of 99.7 ± 0.2% and a large linear shrinkage of 23.5 ± 0.1%."

item.intervention: Homogenization at 1500 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching
item.processing: Homogenization at 1500 °C for 1 h, water quenching
item.structure_change: Metastable single β-BCC phase obtained (with residual HfC); α-HCP phase disappears
item.property_change: Hardness increases compared to multiphase sintered sample
item.attributed_mechanism: α-to-β transition temperature is between 1280 °C and 1500 °C at 0.996 wt.% O; Hf and Zr diffusion into β-BCC matrix contributes to solid-solution strengthening
quotes: A metastable single β‐BCC phase (with residual HfC) is obtained after quenching, as shown in the XRD spectrum of Figure 3b.

After quenching, the metastable single β‐BCC sample shows a higher hardness than the multiphase, sintered sample, for two possible reasons: a) Hf and Zr diffused into the β‐BCC matrix and contribute to substitutional solid‐solution strengthening
This indicates that the α‐to‐β transition temperature should be between 1280 °C (extrapolated from the guideline) and 1500 °C at our oxygen concentration of 0.996 wt.%.

item.processing: Uniaxial compression at 1000 °C, strain rate 10^-4 s^-1
item.structure_change: Cracks forming along shearing bands observed on heavily deformed sample
item.property_change: Yield strength much higher than arc-melted HfNbTaTiZr (750–1100 °C); stress drop after yielding observed
item.attributed_mechanism: Interstitial strengthening from oxygen (≈1.0 wt.%) and carbon; dynamic recovery and recrystallization contribute to stress drop; cracks in shearing bands contribute to softening
quotes: Figure 4a,b shows that the yield strength is much higher for sintered HfNbTaTiZr bulk than for arc‐melted HfNbTaTiZr reported in Refs. [ [25] , [45] ] between 750 to 1100 °C.

This indicates that oxygen interstitial strengthening may significantly increase yield strength in the current HfNbTaTiZr samples: using the above equations provides strengthening contributions of 676 and 95 MPa, respectively.
In addition, cracks forming along shearing bands, observed on the heavily deformed sample (inset in Figure 4a ), may also have contributed to the softening of the flow stress.

item.processing: Uniaxial compression at 800–1000 °C, strain rate 10^-4 s^-1
item.structure_change: Lattices compressed without fracture up to 50%; barreling behavior at 900 °C; brooming behavior at 1000 °C for ρ=51% sample
item.property_change: Yield strength decreases with temperature; lattices show higher specific yield strength than Inconel 718 above 900 °C
item.attributed_mechanism: Dynamic recovery and recrystallization become dominant at 900 °C; progressive densification competes with softening; high tensile ductility at high temperatures
quotes: As shown in Figure 4c,d , the sintered lattice can be compressed without fracture up to 50% between 800 and 1000 °C.
A decrease of stress after yielding is observed beginning at 900 °C, indicating that dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallization may become dominant at this temperature
The sintered lattices have a higher specific yield strength than Inconel 718 above 900 °C.

item.intervention: Oxidation test at 1000 °C for 20 h under flowing air
item.processing: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) at 1000 °C, 50 mL min^-1 air flow
item.structure_change: Uncoated sample pulverized (pestering); silicide-coated sample maintains shape with white/yellow regions; (Zr,Hf)O2 fills cracks in coating
item.property_change: Parabolic rate constant k for uncoated sample is 570 mg^2 cm^-4 h^-1, ≈700 times higher than coated sample (0.80 mg^2 cm^-4 h^-1); mass gain of uncoated sample (148 mg cm^-2) is ≈30 times higher than coated (5.2 mg cm^-2) after 10 h
item.attributed_mechanism: Silicide coating inhibits oxidation; self-healing mechanism where (Zr,Hf)O2 fills cracks and Si diffuses deeper, preventing run-away oxidation
quotes: The parabolic rate constant k is directly related to the self‐diffusion coefficient of oxygen (or metallic elements) in the oxide scale and thus fully describes the oxidation kinetics during the early stage growth of the oxide layer.

The parabolic rate constant k is directly related to the self‐diffusion coefficient of oxygen (or metallic elements) in the oxide scale and thus fully describes the oxidation kinetics during the early stage growth of the oxide layer.
The mass of the uncoated sample becomes stable after 12 h due to the completion of oxidation.

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Uncoated vs. Silicide-coated HfNbTaTiZr. Intervention: Oxidation test at 1000 °C for 20 h under flowing air. Processing: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) at 1000 °C, 50 mL min^-1 air flow. Test conditions: 1000 °C, flowing air, 20 h. Mechanism: Silicide coating inhibits oxidation; self-healing mechanism where (Zr,Hf)O2 fills cracks and Si diffuses deeper, preventing run-away oxidation. Evidence: measured. Quote: "The parabolic rate constant k is directly related to the self‐diffusion coefficient of oxygen (or metallic elements) in the oxide scale and thus fully describes the oxidation kinetics during the early stage growth of the oxide layer."

item.structure_change: Pre-existing cracks filled with (Zr,Hf)O2; Si released and diffuses deeper; SiO2 particles observed within oxide inclusions
item.attributed_mechanism: Zr and Hf react with oxygen to form oxide while Si is released and diffuses deeper; SiO2 particles relieve stress between oxide grains by viscous flow
quotes: Thus, Zr and Hf within the silicide coating react with oxygen to form the oxide, while Si is released and diffuses deeper in the specimen, increasing the depth of the coating.
